@@7270941 <h> New study tracks nitrogen footprint of products made for export <p> Just four countries -- the US , China , India and Brazil -- are responsible for almost half of the world 's total nitrogen pollution , a new study finds . <p> The new research maps the nitrogen ' footprint ' of 188 countries , and finds that around a quarter of emissions come from making products that are then traded internationally . <p> As most of this trade takes products from poorer countries to richer ones , nitrogen pollution in developing nations is being driven by demand for food and clothing products in developed countries , the researchers say . <h> Nitrogen footprint <p> Nitrogen pollution comes in various different forms . Some of the main sources are from burning fossil fuels in cars and power stations ( nitrogen oxides ) , processing of textiles for clothing ( nitrous oxide ) , rearing livestock and using fertilisers ( nitrous oxide and ammonia ) , and water run-off from industry and farming taking nitrogen into water supplies . <p> Nitrogen emissions have a number of impacts @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Arunima Malik , a PhD student in the Integrated Sustainability Analysis group at the University of Sydney , who co-authored the new Nature Geoscience study . She tells Carbon Brief : <p> Some of the impacts include air pollution ( leading to respiratory illnesses ) , acid rain , eutrophication water pollution from high nutrient levels , and climate change . Nitrates from fertilisers can pollute groundwater -- some agricultural areas are suffering so much that locals need to buy bottled water because tap water is unsafe for human consumption . <p> The study takes all the different forms of nitrogen emissions and converts them into a single figure , which they call a nitrogen ' footprint ' . On a global scale , the average person has a nitrogen footprint of 27kg per year , says the study , but the size of emissions -- both per person and as national totals -- varies hugely across the world . <p> Top of the per person polluting pile is Hong Kong at 225kg per year , followed by the Netherlands at 140kg , and Kuwait at 100kg . The UK comes @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ around double the global average . At the other end of the scale are Liberia , Moldova and C ? te d'Ivoire , each with emissions of less than 7kg per person per year . <p> Richer countries tend to have a larger nitrogen footprint because of their consumption of animal products , processed foods , clothes , and energy-intensive products , the paper says . <p> But as the researchers calculated emissions according to where these products are consumed , rather than produced , the study also reveals that national footprints often extend into other countries . <h> Import and export <p> Combining databases of global emissions and international trade with a global nitrogen cycle model , the researchers tracked where products -- and their emissions -- originate from . As Malik explains : <p> In essence , we scanned and analysed 5bn global supply chains for 15,000 commodities produced in 188 countries . <p> Their findings show that just four countries -- China ( 20% ) , India ( 11% ) , the US ( 10% ) and Brazil ( 6% ) -- make up almost half of global @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the Top 10 -- Russia , Pakistan , Indonesia , Australia , Mexico and Argentina -- make up another 12% . <p> Countries like the US and Russia are " net importers " of nitrogen emissions . This means the nitrogen they emit when producing commodities for export is less than the equivalent emissions for the products they import . For countries such as China and India , the opposite applies -- they are " net exporters " so the total nitrogen emissions are higher for their exports than their imports . <p> Net exporters therefore bear the higher environmental and health costs of nitrogen pollution because they 're producing food and clothing that are consumed in other countries . <p> The chart below shows the world 's Top 10 net importers and net exporters . The bars to the right of the line show nitrogen emissions that are imported , and bars to the left show those exported . Scotland Yard estimated that the crowd numbered 200,000 . The organisers claimed 300,000 . <p> For all their enthusiasm , the marchers had no impact at all on government policy . The land-based missiles to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ because of objectors , but under an international agreement . The Trident missiles are still carried in submarines , though there 's now a debate as to whether they should be renewed . <p> CND may have slipped off the news bulletins , but it never went out of existence . Bruce Kent , the former Roman Catholic priest who was a public face of the 1980s protest , still calls into CND 's north London headquarters a couple of times a week . The coming month will see several events designed to get CND back in the public eye , culminating in a rally in Trafalgar Square on 27 February where the main speaker will be Jeremy Corbyn . Organisers are expecting 50,000 or more . <p> Kate Hudson , long-serving CND general secretary , was a face in the crowd at the 1980s Hyde Park rally . " It was very exciting , " she said . " Those big demonstrations were my first experience of collective resolve . I have a very clear memory of one of those large demonstrations in Hyde Park . We felt that with cruise missiles coming , the Soviets and the US were gearing up to fight their nuclear war in Europe . Now people are thinking more about what is our security threat today . " <p> Also working in CND 's favour is the shift in the political landscape , summed up in two words -- Jeremy Corbyn . He stuck with CND during the wilderness years . This inspired the launch of CND , with the philosopher Bertrand Russell as its president and the Labour MP Michael Foot as a prominent member . <p> But people became accustomed to living with the bomb . But when disarmament talks between the superpowers began in the mid-1980s , CND again went into decline . Unilateralism was a vote loser . @@7300502 <h> Speed comes at a cost <h> John Wylde <p> Transport is one of the most significant users of energy . The recent climate change summit conference in Paris was rather more successful than its predecessor in Copenhagen six years previously , identifying courses of action which we must take if the human race is to survive . <p> People talk about saving the planet , but the planet will keep on rolling more or less whatever we do to it . It is life , and particularly human life , which will cease to exist if we carry on as we are . <p> We have to make major changes . <p> For the first time in history , we are capable of destroying ourselves , and we shall do that if we do not address the issues . <p> It is now generally agreed that man 's own actions have brought about the recent changes in our climate which are resulting in storms and the resulting floods , for example . <p> These changes are only marginal , of course . <p> Climate change has been @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> For example , the last ice age , when almost all of Britain was covered with ice , receded 10,000 years ago , and the climate may be still be getting warmer in its natural 100,000-year cycle , in which case our actions have simply accelerated the process , whereas it would be better if we tried to retard it . <p> One of the largest users of energy is conflict , and one of the most effective ways of saving humanity would be to stop it , but as it has been a feature of our existence forever , there seems little likelihood of that being achievable . <p> Less than 200 years ago , the Industrial Revolution resulted in the burning of huge amounts of coal , much of it by steam engines on railways and in ships . <p> A little over 100 years ago the discovery of oil and the invention of the internal combustion engine led to the massive expansion of road and air transport . <p> One of the outcomes of the Paris talks was the greater realisation that our survival will depend @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ energy . <p> In Britain , this realisation unfortunately coincided with the Government 's decision to massively reduce support for carbon capture and renewable sources of energy , such as solar power , and to encourage and even promote the development of marginal sources of non-renewables by means of fracking . <p> The development of electric cars does seem to be making some progress now , and even electric buses , but the size and weight of the batteries which would be needed to power a large lorry means that there is apparently no progress in this sector yet , although there has been some experimentation in aviation in the form of a solar-powered light aircraft , which has made some long flights , and experiments in using wind power to assist the progress of large ships have taken several forms . <p> All forms of experimentation are beneficial , because they will be developed until they become fully functional , so we can look forward to major changes in most forms of transport during the coming century . <p> Our railways are still much too heavily dependent on diesel power @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ more than half a century . <p> Even now , when its importance is beginning to be recognised , progress is still lacking in urgency . Lead times in the railway industry are such that to achieve something within a decade is really quick . <p> Much of the current activity on the railways stems from the non-political appointment by Labour in 2009 of Lord Adonis as transport secretary . His initiatives were fortunately carried on by the coalition government the following year . <p> The railways have always sought to improve their efficiency , as all good businesses should , significantly by increasing speed . <p> The justification for HS2 is that it will accelerate movement between London and the major conurbations in the north , including Scotland , by providing a high-speed line bypassing the congested , current routes between London , Birmingham , Manchester and Leeds . <p> However , there is a paradox here as increased speed means increased energy consumption , which is now a separate consideration , and speed has to be balanced with the use of energy . <p> Half a century ago , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ cost . As part of the strategy for high-speed trains , there was a development called the Advanced Passenger Train ( APT ) , which included a tilting mechanism to enable it to go round sharp curves faster without upsetting the passengers . <p> There were several versions , using different forms of propulsion . <p> This train included so much new technology that it took time to develop , so some of the railway engineers devised a simpler , quicker solution to speed things up and called it the High Speed Train ( HST ) . <p> The first of these entered service in 1976 and were a huge success . Most are due to be withdrawn by 2020 , to be replaced by the InterCity Express , which is being built at Shildon in County Durham . <p> By coincidence , one of the Advanced Passenger Train prototypes is housed in the National Rail Museum 's annex at Shildon , as shown in the accompanying image . <p> Clearly , the styling experts did not get to work on it before it was withdrawn . <p> The reason it @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ at a bad time , in midwinter , when the weather really took a turn for the worse , and things went badly wrong on the demonstration run for the press . <p> Resultant bad publicity led to the withdrawal of government funding and the sale of the technology to Fiat , which was already making trains designed on the same principle called Pendolinos . <p> The Italian firm incorporated the British technology into a new design and sold it to various railways , including Virgin Trains for use on the west coast main line in Britain . <p> This website and its associated newspaper adheres to the Independent Press Standards Organisation 's Editors ' Code of Practice . The international ensemble of actors brings vividly to life the struggle to think about what 's ahead when social conditioning has us checking our phones in the face of crisis . <p> This February , discover the latest emerging talent from The Royal Central School of Speech and Drama over an eleven day run at the Tristan Bates Theatre in the heart of Covent Garden . <p> Graduating actors from the BA ( Hons ) Acting Collaborative and Devised Theatre course have worked alongside BA ( Hons ) Theatre Practice students and industry professionals to create a dynamic piece of new , original new work . <p> In this premier performance run , This Is Not A Drill explores themes of the future , the rise of the digital age , climate change , space travel and galactic possibilities . Combining bold , innovative use of video , light @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ with rigorous contemporary questioning , the show pushes the boundaries for new work by young theatre makers . <p> Professional support includes direction by Jemima James ( Assistant Director on Complicite 's The Encounter ) and set and costume design by Harry Whitham ( Hookup by Outbox at Hackney Showroom ) . <p> About This Is Not A Drill <p> It 's undeniable . The future is coming . Red lines on graphs and water levels are rising and smart blue screens are getting smarter by the second . The big cars with tinted windows are driving past tired people walking along the roadside . The supersize bite of progress does n't taste quite the same as it did before . <p> This is not a drill takes us on a journey across Outer and Inner Space , cyber landscapes and the kitchen floor . The international ensemble of actors brings vividly to life the struggle to think about what 's ahead when social conditioning has us checking our phones in the face of crisis . The result is darkly funny , highly theatrical , intelligent and surprising . Directed by @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ by the company . Presented by The Royal Central School of Speech and Drama . <p> About The Royal Central School of Speech and Drama <p> The Royal Central School of Speech and Drama is a higher education conservatoire - a specialist college nurturing creative collaboration . Courses include acting , applied theatre , movement , musical theatre , drama &amp; movement therapy , theatre &amp; live performance , puppetry , scenography , actor &amp; teacher training , voice , technical arts &amp; production , and writing for stage &amp; broadcast media . With over 60 academic staff , together with visiting artists and lecturers , Central has the largest grouping of **25;403;TOOLONG specialists in the UK , an active research culture and is a hub for the theatre and performance industries . Central is HEFCE 's only designated Centre for Excellence in Training for Theatre . <p> Central 's Acting Collaborative and Devised Theatre course is innovative and rigorous , emphasising the creation of new theatre and embracing a multi-cultural and multi-disciplinary methodology . Students graduate with the skills to work in classical and contemporary theatre , film , radio @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ work . <p> The course is led by Catherine Alexander , associate director with Complicite , and is taught by a range of award-winning professional directors and teachers . From the outset , the course works closely with professional theatre companies and emergent or professionally active directors . Recently , students have had workshops and created performances with Complicite , Nancy Meckler , Filter Theatre , Declan Donnellan , Max Stafford-Clark , Robin Soans , Tanika Gupta , Douglas Rintoul/Transport Theatre , John Wright and Blind Summit . <p> This is Not a Drill , an original new theatre work created by the company over a five week period , encapsulates the ethos of the course : collaborative , experimental and interdisciplinary .
